rv.q: An anatomy of power and cruelty among the privileged, Angel’s Bone offers a powerful, painful experience.
The production is dizzyingly full-on, our attention fractured by the spinning stage, split screens and steadicam operators stealthily racing around like dark, voyeuristic angels.
Angel’s Bone kicks off the season with a powerful boot to the solar plexus.
Frustratingly, while the storytelling is admirably clear, the endlessly rotating walls are problematic, forming an impenetrable barrier that even obscures the screens at times.
Ultimately, the work confronts its audience with horrors, but often falls into excess, pushing the core message further away.
If only the American Pulitzer prize-winning opera Angel’s Bone had been worth the elaborate effort.
It’s quite testing, but I’m glad I’ve seen it.
Du Yun’s music is kaleidoscopic in nature, drawing on a variety of styles from cool modernism to pounding rock, and consequently offers something for almost everyone.
ENO went bleak, some went home unexpectedly early but those that stayed saw something that shifted the boundaries of modern opera.
There is no doubt it is a compelling production, if not exactly an enjoyable one.
But influencer culture is an absurdly easy target, and it’s at this stage that what at first promised to be profound in Angel’s Bones now reveals itself to be shallow and overblown.
I don't think I have been this engrossed in a piece of theatre for such a long time.
Superbly sung and staged, the London premiere of the Pulitzer Prize-winning opera is visceral and thought-provoking...
The work of everyone on stage and off is exemplary.
And with outstandingly committed performances from everyone on stage and off, I can only admire Du Yun, Vavrek and ENO for their courage in putting on this show.
The musical team brought together for this production is remarkable.
Much of the time in this instance one feels as if one’s being drip fed poison.
Whether all these musical elements come together to form an entirely convincing whole is another question, but there’s no denying the composer’s imagination or her willingness to push boundaries.
This is a difficult and important subject, but one that is made more difficult and ultimately unrewarding by its handling.
It’s impressively executed with all the panache, commitment, and technical excellence that we have come to expect from ENO, but overall is somehow rather disappointing.
Williams’ bold production is a technical marvel, but it’s hard to imagine anyone but the greatest theatrophiles connecting to this story in its current form.
While the subject matter undoubtedly demands a confronting approach, one can find themselves wishing that some of these moments had been explored through a different, perhaps more symbolic lens.

cn.t: Du Yun's Pulitzer-winning opera about human trafficking earns praise for its bold performances and visceral staging, but divides critics over its heavy-handed approach and overwhelming multimedia production.
